idiom_name: EF Core DbContext change tracker + SaveChanges (automatic transaction)
implementation_notes: EF Core's DbContext is the unit of work and its own documentation says so - 'DbContext is designed to represent a short-lived unit-of-work'. Entity instances become tracked when they are returned from a query or attached with Add/Attach/Update, DetectChanges compares current values against the original snapshot at SaveChanges time, and SaveChanges applies every pending insert, update and delete inside one transaction by default. That replaces the classic register/flush structure entirely: you mutate tracked entities and call SaveChangesAsync once per business operation. ADO.NET (SqlConnection.BeginTransaction plus SqlTransaction.Commit/Rollback, with commands enlisted through their Transaction property) is the manual base layer for code that wants explicit SQL and its own change list.
code_sketch:
await using var ctx = new BlogsContext();          // the unit of work
var blog = await ctx.Blogs.FirstAsync(b => b.Id == 1);
blog.Name = ".NET Blog (Updated!)";                 // tracked, no SQL yet
ctx.Posts.Add(new Post { Title = "New" });         // Insert at flush
ctx.Remove(oldPost);                               // Delete at flush
await ctx.SaveChangesAsync();                      // one transaction
// ctx.ChangeTracker.DetectChanges() + DebugView shows Added/Modified/Deleted
pitfalls: A long-lived DbContext keeps growing its change tracker (memory) and serves stale entities; the documented lifetime is create, track, mutate, SaveChanges, dispose.
Calling SaveChanges twice splits one business transaction into two commits; if you need a wider boundary, wrap both calls in an explicit Database.BeginTransactionAsync.
DbContext is not thread-safe and does not support concurrent operations; parallel work needs separate contexts or the pooling factory.
AutoTransactionBehavior.Never can leave partial changes when SaveChanges needs several commands, since earlier commands are already committed.

variants.name: ADO.NET SqlTransaction with a hand-written change set
variants.implementation_notes: Without an ORM the pattern is hand-written over ADO.NET: open one SqlConnection, call BeginTransaction, enlist every command through its Transaction property (the provider throws if a command runs on a connection with an active transaction and no transaction assigned), and keep your own new/dirty/removed lists that are walked in order before Commit. Use this when the application is deliberately statement-oriented (bulk loads, vendor-specific SQL) and an ORM would hide the control you need.
pitfalls: Forgetting to assign the transaction to a command throws InvalidOperationException; the failure mode is loud, but it appears only when the transaction is active.
The in-memory change list is not reverted by Rollback - clear or discard it, or the next flush re-applies rolled-back values.
